### S-01 {#s-01}

**Claim.** Softmax is invariant to a constant shift applied to every logit; only relative logit values matter.

**Source.** Mathematical identity

**Where.** Verified numerically by scripts/check\_softmax\_reference.py

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Purely mathematical; not attributed to a video source. Checked by script, not by citation.

**Claim.** Temperature rescales logits before softmax normalization; as T approaches 0 the distribution converges to argmax when there is a unique highest logit; as T approaches infinity the distribution approaches uniform.

**Where.** Video, ~22:22, "Softmax with temperature"

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** The tie case for T to 0 is stated on this site; not necessarily discussed at this timestamp in the video.

### S-09 {#s-09}

**Claim.** In this course, 'logit' means the network's raw, pre-softmax real-valued score. This is not the same object as the statistics/econometrics logit function, logit(p) = log(p/(1-p)), the log-odds transform of an already-computed probability. The relationship is exact only for differences: under softmax with temperature T, log(p\_i/p\_j) = (z\_i - z\_j)/T, and for exactly two candidates logit(p\_1) = (z\_1 - z\_2)/T, which reduces to z\_1 - z\_2 only at T = 1. An individual multiclass score z\_i is not logit(p\_i).

**Source.** Mathematical definition

**Where.** Definitional comparison plus the algebraic identity log(p\_i/p\_j) = (z\_i - z\_j)/T, which follows directly from the softmax formula; verified numerically at T=1 for the module's five-token example (log(p\_1/p\_2) = 1.0 = z\_1 - z\_2).

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Terminological clarification; both definitions are independently verifiable standard usage, not attributed to one external source. Corrected 2026-09-15: an earlier wording said the two 'share a name and a family resemblance, not an object', which understated the exact two-candidate relationship.

### S-10 {#s-10}

**Claim.** Softmax is named by contrast with the hard argmax (picking the single top-scoring candidate and giving it everything): softmax returns a whole probability distribution rather than the maximum value or its index, is smooth and differentiable everywhere, and approaches the argmax's one-hot choice in the T-to-0 limit derived in this module.

**Source.** Mathematical identity / standard ML terminology

**Where.** Naming convention; verifiable directly from the T-to-0 limit already derived in this module's temperature section.

**Support.** inference; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Naming convention, not a citation to one paper or video. Corrected 2026-09-15: earlier wording said 'max/argmax'; softmax is the smooth counterpart of the one-hot argmax indicator, not of the maximum value (the smooth counterpart of the maximum value is log-sum-exp).

### S-11 {#s-11}

**Claim.** 'Temperature' is borrowed from the statistical-mechanics Boltzmann distribution, p\_i proportional to exp(-E\_i/(kT)): high T flattens the distribution over states, low T concentrates it on the lowest-energy state. Softmax-with-temperature has the same structure, with a logit playing the role of a negative energy.

**Source.** Standard statistical mechanics (Boltzmann distribution)

**Where.** General physics identity, independently verifiable in any statistical-mechanics reference.

**Support.** inference; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Not attributed to S1 or S2 in this repository's source set; this etymology has not been independently confirmed as explicitly stated in either video.

### S-14 {#s-14}

**Claim.** Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter via the chain rule in one backward sweep; it does not, by itself, change any parameter. A separate optimizer step (e.g. plain gradient descent, or a more sophisticated rule such as Adam) uses those gradients to update the parameters.

**Source.** Mathematical identity / standard definition

**Where.** Correction CC5 (adopted at external review); verified numerically by scripts/check\_neuron\_example.py

**Support.** inference; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Distinguishes two logically separate steps sometimes conflated in casual description; standard in any optimization or deep-learning reference.

### S-15 {#s-15}

**Claim.** Composing affine layers (weighted sum plus bias), with no nonlinearity, yields a function that is itself affine in the input regardless of depth; a nonlinear activation breaks that restriction and allows a multi-layer network to represent nonlinear relationships an affine model cannot.

**Source.** Mathematical identity

**Where.** Linear algebra: composition of affine maps is affine.

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Reworded 2026-09-15 from 'linear' to 'affine' because the lesson's layers carry biases.

### S-16 {#s-16}

**Claim.** Vaswani et al., Table 1, reports for a Recurrent layer: complexity per layer O(n times d-squared), a minimum of O(n) sequential operations, and a maximum path length of O(n), where n is sequence length and d is representation dimension. Section 1 states that this sequential dependency 'precludes parallelization within training examples.' For a toy chain of n=8 positions, the maximum path length between the two most distant positions is 7 sequential steps and processing the sequence once requires 8 sequential steps -- this course's own concrete instantiation of the paper's O(n) bound, not a number stated by the paper itself.

**Source.** Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762, v7, 2023-08-02)

**Where.** Section 1 (paragraph 2) and Section 4 ("Why Self-Attention"), Table 1, Recurrent row

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Verified directly against the live paper (PDF) on 2026-09-14. The n=8 concrete figures are this course's own arithmetic instantiation of the stated asymptotic bound, checked by scripts/check\_transformer\_path\_lengths.py.

### S-17 {#s-17}

**Claim.** Vaswani et al., Table 1, reports for a Self-Attention layer: complexity per layer O(n-squared times d), O(1) sequential operations, and O(1) maximum path length -- a self-attention layer connects any two positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, independent of their distance. Section 4 states the reason path length matters: 'The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies.' The O(n-squared times d) figure is self-attention's arithmetic cost per layer, not a claim about any particular implementation's memory use.

**Source.** Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need"

**Where.** Section 4 ("Why Self-Attention"), Table 1, Self-Attention row, and the paragraph following the three desiderata

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Verified directly against the live paper (PDF) on 2026-09-14; the Section 4 'shorter these paths' sentence verified verbatim against the arXiv HTML (v7) on 2026-09-14. The n=8 concrete figures are this course's own arithmetic instantiation, checked by scripts/check\_transformer\_path\_lengths.py. No implementation-memory claim is made from this row; FlashAttention and similar techniques are out of scope for this batch (see docs/decisions.md). Under causal masking the constant path holds for every permitted (earlier-to-later) pair, which is what an autoregressive model needs.

This course does not evaluate or endorse any specific alternative.

### S-86 {#s-86}

**Claim.** An embedding lookup is mathematically equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector (all zeros except a single one at the token's index) by the embedding matrix E: the product selects the row E\[i\]. Implementations simply retrieve the row.

**Source.** Mathematical identity

**Where.** Linear algebra: for the standard basis vector e\_i, e\_i^T E equals the i-th row of E.

**Support.** direct; confidence high.

**Caveat.** Purely mathematical; stated on short-story.qmd §4 as an optional aside. Not attributed to any external source.
